body:
`person:seth-klarman` | confidence: **verified** | tags: us, process, value, avoid-ruin

Founded Baupost (1982/83). Record varies by window: ~19% net a year vs 11% for the S&P 500 to 2010 (Bloomberg); 'just over 20%' with one losing year (Ivey); 16.4% to end-2015 (CNBC); but only ~4% a year since 2014 per investors, with clients pulling ~$7bn since 2021 (Bloomberg, Jan 2025). Structural edge: patient endowment-style capital (Harvard-type LPs) that let him hold large cash (often 30-50%) and buy illiquid, complex assets others are forced to sell - bankruptcy claims (e.g., Lehman claims after 2008), distressed debt, post-reorganisation equities, real estate. Process: absolute-return mindset; buy at a big discount to conservatively estimated value; focus on downside first; catalysts help; avoid leverage. His 1991 book Margin of Safety is out of print. Mistakes: long cash drag in a decade-long bull market; post-2014 performance shows an edge in distress needs distress to exist. Copyable: write down the downside value first; accept holding cash when nothing is cheap; hunt for forced sellers (index deletions, spin-offs, rights issues, promoters under margin call, MF redemptions in smallcaps) - India's 2018 and 2020 smallcap selloffs were Klarman-style opportunities. Not copyable: buying Lehman claims.

| key | value |
|---|---|
| track_record | ~19-20% net 1983-2010; 16.4% to 2015; ~4%/yr since 2014 (Bloomberg) |
| source_quality | press + LP-reported; Baupost does not publish |
| mistakes | cash drag, post-2014 lag |
| copyable | downside-first, forced-seller hunting, permission to hold cash |

Links: strategy:klarman-margin-of-safety (about); insight:avoid-ruin (illustrates)

Sources: <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2010-06-17/the-financial-life-seth-klarman> ; <https://ivey.uwo.ca/bengrahaminvesting/resources/interviews-notes/seth-a-klarman> ; <https://www.cnbc.com/2016/08/30/how-to-think-like-value-investing-idol-seth-klarman.html> ; <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-01-22/baupost-clients-pulled-7-billion-since-2021-after-poor-returns>

body:
1. **No rule passes the pre-registered bar.** For every rule P(flagged → >3x) is *at or above* the base rate
   (ANY: 64% vs 51% unflagged, p = 0.009), so by decision rule 2 none qualifies as a hard filter on this sample,
   and none reaches 2x base loss rate with p < 0.05 at 5 years. The R3 auditor rule is the closest on the
   *to-date* horizon (4 of 31 flagged firms down >50% vs 3.3%, p = 0.027), but to-date wasn't the primary
   horizon and n = 4.
2. **The test can barely see losers.** Base rate of a >50% 5-year loss is **1.8% (9 of 495)**. Two reasons, both
   biases stated in advance: survivors only (the Gensols, Cox & Kings and DHFLs of 2020 aren't in a list drawn in
   2023), and Sep-2020 was close to the COVID low before a five-year small-cap bull run (median stock 3.3x).
3. **A second selection bias favours flagged firms:** the PEAD sample kept only firms whose mcap reached Rs 400 cr
   *at some point in 2018–2025*. A tiny, pledged, cash-poor firm in 2020 got in only if it later grew. Firms
   under Rs 400 cr at T0 tripled 72% of the time vs 44% for firms already above it. Restricting to mcap ≥ Rs 400 cr
   at T0 shrinks the "flagged firms do better" effect (ANY x3 57% vs 41%, p = 0.027) but doesn't reverse it, and
   pledge > 50% then shows the only material loss lift: **10% vs 1.4% (2 of 20), p = 0.053** — Sadbhav
   Engineering/Sadbhav Infra (pledges 56% / 82%, −76%).
4. **Names behind the numbers.** Of the 9 >50% 5-year losers, ANY fired on 4: Sadbhav Engineering and Sadbhav
   Infra (pledge 56% / 82%), JHS (cash conversion), SecureKloud (auditor resignation 2019). Den, Radio City, Take
   Solutions and Valiant Organics fired nothing (GVP Tech had no data). On the to-date horizon ZEEL (−63%) fired
   nothing at T0 because its pledge had already been invoked down to 16% of a 4.8% promoter stake — the damage
   was done. Flagged *winners* include CG Power (auditor exit
   in 2020 mid-fraud discovery, then a Murugappa takeover: ~31x), Ramky (auditor exit 2015, ~19x), Aurionpro and
   TI. A flag at a distressed low often marks a *bottom*, after the bad news was public and priced.
5. **What Part B can't tell us:** whether the rules would have saved us from the delisted traps (they aren't in
   the data), and how they behave from a market peak. A fair Part B needs a point-in-time universe that keeps
   dead companies (stage 1: Screener login + delisted-company lists) and several snapshot dates (2017-12, 2019-06,
   2021-12, 2023-12).

body:
`size = min(kelly_fraction × f*, tier cap at cost, liquidity cap)`, then 0 if any gate blocks.
- `f*` maximises `E[ln(1 + f·(M/H − 1))]` over the scenario outcomes (each spread by 5-point Gauss-Hermite on σ, with the blow-up as a point mass). `H` is the index hurdle multiple, so the bet is measured against the alternative.
- Kelly fraction defaults to 0.25 (`strategy:thorp-kelly`).
- Tier caps (`strategy:position-sizing`): core 5%, satellite 4%, speculative 2%.
- Liquidity cap = `adv_pct × ADV × days_to_exit ÷ portfolio value`, in the same money units.
- Phase A: every size is a **paper size**. In practice mode the card says that this is a mechanical rule output, not a size for anyone.
